allOf.description: Inherits shared step-base properties ($schema, id, owner, created_at, canonical_refs_used).

trace.description: Traceability links connecting this red team assessment to the capabilities and APIs it covers. Every threat must trace to at least one upstream capability or API it targets. type = the canonical kind of the target: use type='capability' for cap-* IDs, type='api' for api-* IDs. The relationship verb (derives_from) goes in note. Example: [{"type": "capability", "id": "cap-user-authentication", "note": "derives_from: threat targets the credential validation flow"}]. Threats without trace links cannot be validated against the attack surface defined in Steps 01–05. Multiple traces allowed when a threat crosses capability boundaries.

items.description: A single traceability reference. At step 11, type = the canonical kind of the target: use type='api' for api-* IDs, type='capability' for cap-* IDs. The relationship verb (derives_from) goes in note. Example: {"type": "api", "id": "api-session-create", "note": "derives_from: token forgery and session fixation threats target this endpoint"}. Anti-pattern: type='implements' or type='derives_from' — these are relationship verbs, not canonical kinds; type must be the kind of the target artifact.

threats.description: Identified security threats with severity, mitigations, and traceability. Must contain at least one threat (enforced by minItems).

threat_id.description: Unique kebab-case identifier for this threat. Recommended format: threat-{category}-{description}. Example: 'threat-auth-token-forgery', 'threat-data-sql-injection', 'threat-dos-api-flooding'. Should be stable across spec versions.

description.description: Human-readable threat name and scenario summary. A threat description is specific enough when it names: (1) the attacker's entry point (which API, field, or component), (2) the attack technique, and (3) what the attacker gains if successful. Examples: 'JWT Token Forgery via Algorithm Confusion — attacker crafts a token with alg:none to bypass signature validation on the /api/session endpoint, gaining unauthenticated access as any user', 'SQL Injection via Unparameterized Search Query — attacker injects UNION SELECT into the q parameter of GET /api/search to exfiltrate the users table'. Anti-pattern: 'System might be vulnerable to injection attacks' (too vague — does not name the entry point, technique, or impact).

vector.description: Attack vector or method by which the threat could be exploited. Describe the attacker's entry point, technique, and preconditions. Example: 'Attacker crafts a JWT with alg=none header bypassing signature verification on the token validation middleware'. The vector should be specific enough that a penetration tester could begin probing immediately. Anti-pattern: 'via the API' (too generic — name the specific endpoint, field, or header); 'through user input' (does not specify which input or which manipulation).

target_ids.description: Trace references to spec artifacts this threat targets. Valid target types are: api (api_id from Step 05) and component (component_id from Step 02). Each threat must target at least one concrete artifact (enforced by minItems) — generic 'the whole system' threats are not actionable. Targeting specific APIs and components enables cross-referencing with Step 05 interface contracts and Step 02 system sketch.

items.description: A trace reference to a specific spec artifact (API from Step 05 or component from Step 02) targeted by this threat.

category.description: Security domain category with one concrete example per value: 'authn' — JWT algorithm confusion attack where an attacker signs a token with 'alg: none'; 'authz' — IDOR via direct object reference where a user accesses another user's order by incrementing the ID; 'business_logic' — double-charge in a payment flow triggered by rapid duplicate POST requests; 'transport' — MITM attack stripping HTTPS to HTTP at a misconfigured proxy; 'data_privacy' — PII exposure in verbose error messages that include email addresses and stack traces. When a threat spans categories, assign the category of the primary attack surface. Anti-pattern: using 'transport' for network-level data leakage (that is 'data_privacy' if the data is the target, 'transport' only if the attack is the network path itself). Do NOT use expanded or alternate forms — they will fail enum validation.

mitigations.description: Structured mitigations for this threat. Each mitigation should be a concrete action, not a vague aspiration. Include: (1) a specific technical or process control, (2) where it is applied (component, layer, or process), (3) how effectiveness is measured. Example: 'Apply HMAC-SHA256 signature verification on all incoming webhooks at the API gateway layer. Verified by integration test fix-05-webhook-tampered'. Mitigations must be structured objects — not plain strings. Valid mitigation target types: inv-* (invariant from Step 06 — adds an invariant to prevent the threat), nfr-* (NFR from Step 07 — adds a performance/security requirement), fr-* (FR from Step 04 — adds a functional requirement to address the threat), doc (net-new proposed control or documentation-based mitigation that has no existing upstream spec ID; exempt from cross-reference validation because there is no doc-ID registry in the toolkit). Each mitigation must reference an existing artifact ID. Anti-pattern: listing a mitigation without a target ID ('add input validation' with no fr-* or inv-* reference — not traceable to a spec change).

type.description: The artifact type that provides the mitigation (e.g., 'fr' for a functional requirement, 'inv' for an invariant, 'fixture' for a test fixture). For type 'capability', the id should reference a cap-* ID from Step 01 capabilities. Use 'doc' for a net-new proposed control or documentation-based mitigation that has no existing upstream spec ID; 'doc' mitigations are exempt from cross-reference validation because there is no doc-ID registry in the toolkit.

id.description: Kebab-case ID of the mitigating artifact. Should match a valid ID in the referenced artifact type's spec file (validated by linters).

note.description: Specific explanation of how this artifact mitigates the threat — include the control mechanism, layer of application, and how effectiveness is verified.

items.description: A structured mitigation linking a concrete spec artifact to this threat. Must specify artifact type, artifact ID, and optionally a note explaining the control.

severity.description: Risk level for this threat. Calibrate using these concrete scenario anchors: 'critical' — auth bypass allows unauthenticated access to all user data or system compromise (e.g., admin takeover); 'high' — authenticated attacker can exfiltrate a significant data set or escalate privileges without additional prerequisites; 'medium' — authenticated attacker can exploit a vulnerability with 2+ additional steps required (requires specific account permissions or unusual timing); 'low' — verbose error messages expose internal paths or versions, exploitable only with significant reconnaissance. Anti-pattern: assigning 'critical' to all threats (use the scenarios above to calibrate — most threats are 'high' or 'medium').

risk_category_ref.description: Canonical reference to the risk category in the canonical registry. Kind must be 'risk_category'. Example: {"id": "cn:core:risk_category:security", "kind": "risk_category", "label": "security"}. Registered core IDs: 'cn:core:risk_category:security', 'cn:core:risk_category:data-privacy', 'cn:core:risk_category:business-logic', 'cn:core:risk_category:data-integrity', 'cn:core:risk_category:authz', 'cn:core:risk_category:delivery-risk'. Must exist in canon/manifest.json before authoring (resolve there, or add a new entry via canonical_proposals + canon-accept) — validated by canonical-integrity lint (E110).

policy_ref.description: Canonical reference to the security policy that mandates this threat be assessed. Kind must be 'policy'. Example: for a JWT attack threat → {"id": "cn:core:policy:authn-required", "kind": "policy", "label": "authn-required"}. Distinguish from risk_category_ref: policy_ref identifies the governance requirement to assess this category; risk_category_ref identifies the risk domain of the specific threat. Include policy_ref when a compliance mandate (SOC2, PCI-DSS) requires assessing this category. Anti-pattern: using the same id for both policy_ref and risk_category_ref.

items.description: A single security threat with severity, mitigations, and targeted artifact IDs.

edge_cases.description: Anomalous inputs or boundary conditions that are not severe enough to be a named threat but could expose unexpected system behaviour under adversarial conditions. Decision rule: document edge cases when: (a) the input is valid by schema but semantically unexpected (empty password, 0-quantity cart), (b) boundary values produce different code paths (exactly at a rate limit, exactly at a max file size), or (c) state sequences are unusual but reachable (accessing a soft-deleted resource, double-submitting a form). Do not duplicate named threat scenarios here.

id.description: Unique kebab-case identifier for this edge case. Convention: ec-{related-threat-id-or-topic}-{n}. Examples: 'ec-session-create-empty-password', 'ec-payment-zero-amount', 'ec-auth-double-submit-1'. If the edge case is related to a named threat, reference the threat ID in the prefix. Anti-pattern: 'ec-1', 'ec-edge-case-3' — sequential labels that cannot be traced to meaning.

description.description: Human-readable description of the anomalous condition and its consequence. Format: '{anomalous input or state} → {expected behaviour} vs {actual/risky behaviour}'. Examples: 'Search query with 10,000-character input bypasses length validation and triggers a 500 error instead of a 400 validation failure', 'Session token presented 1ms after expiry is accepted due to clock skew tolerance exceeding security threshold', 'Cart quantity set to -1 passes schema validation and creates a negative-amount charge'. Anti-pattern: 'Edge case for login' — name the specific anomaly and its consequence.

trigger.description: Description of how to reproduce this edge case — the trigger must be reproducible step-by-step without domain knowledge. Include: (1) exact input format or API call, (2) system state preconditions, (3) sequence of actions. Minimum specificity rule: the trigger must be reproducible — someone reading it must be able to reproduce the edge case without additional context. Good: 'Set JWT alg header to none and remove the signature — send as: eyJ...' (includes exact method). Examples: 'Submit POST /api/search with q parameter set to a 10,001-character string', 'Send authenticated request with token that expires exactly 1 second before the request reaches the validator', 'POST /api/auth/login with Authorization header containing a JWT signed with alg:none — e.g., curl -X POST /api/auth/login -H \'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjoxfQ.\''. Reference the related threat_id if this edge case is a boundary condition of a named threat. Anti-pattern: 'Malformed JWT' (too vague — specify what malformation and how to reproduce it); 'Send unusual request to the API' (not reproducible); omitting the expected vs. actual outcome contrast.

items.description: A single edge case with identifier, description, and optional trigger.
